# Can AI Replace Call Center Agents? What Humans Will Still Do


Evaluate voice AI using your call transcripts. Review short caller responses, find where conversations break down, and improve how your agent listens.


[Max Gibbons](https://www.bland.ai/blog/author/max-gibbons) October 13, 2026


3 min read


AI will eventually handle most call center calls. People will handle the difficult cases and improve the systems taking care of the rest. Teams need to review failed calls, fix missed context, and give people a way to take over when the agent reaches its limits.


Listen to the caller. “I need to move my appointment because my ride can’t get me there until Thursday” gives an agent something to work with. “Scheduling. Appointment. Representative.” tells you the caller has started working around the system.


You can spot that change in a transcript. When someone gives up explaining what they need and starts feeding the phone individual words, you have a conversation worth reviewing.


## **The caller's side of the transcript shows where to look**#


Take a sample from before and after launch. Count caller turns containing one to three words, divide by total caller turns, and record that share for each call. Use the median across the sample so a single long conversation doesn't dominate the result.


Separate tightly framed confirmation prompts from opportunities to explain a problem. Short answers are fine when someone is confirming a date of birth.


A caller who starts with “I need to move my appointment because I can't get a ride until Thursday” and ends up saying “Thursday. Thursday. A person.” has narrowed the search considerably. Listen around the change: an interruption, a missed correction, a question asked again, or an explanation the agent failed to use.


## **The improvement comes from someone reviewing the calls**#


Across the deployments we've reviewed, the improvement loop has a person in it. Someone reviews tagged calls and identifies the failure. An engineer changes the prompt or flow. Another review checks what happened after the change.


One deployment had forty or fifty conversational nodes, each a step where the agent asked, decided, or handed work to the next step. The team identified those handoffs as a leading contributor to hallucination and consolidated the flow to one or two nodes. Three other accounts showed the same fragmentation problem.


For a caller who keeps repeating Thursday, the fix might be preserving a detail across a handoff. For someone repeatedly interrupted, it might be changing when the agent decides to speak. The reviewer can use the transcript to identify the problem and decide what to change.


Review the result alongside the completion and handoff checks in our[IVR versus AI voice agents article](https://www.bland.ai/blog/ivr-vs-ai-voice-agents) , so you can check the caller got help.


## **After launch, the human team often gives the AI less to do**#


We've seen the same direction in post-launch change requests: stop doing arithmetic, stop offering strategy, stop recommending a bid. Teams removed decisions until the agent's behavior became more predictable.


That leaves employees with specific responsibilities: reviewing calls, setting the agent's limits, approving exceptions, and handling requests that need judgment or authority. These are jobs to staff, with time on the schedule and someone accountable for the next review.


The[Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/Office-and-Administrative-Support/Customer-service-representatives.htm) expects automation to reduce demand for some customer-service work while companies continue using people for complex inquiries. In practice, staffing needs to account for the calls that reach people and the work required to keep the automated service improving.


Keep a few before-and-after calls with the change log. On the next review, listen for whether the caller can explain the Thursday constraint once and continue.
